exploration.title: Cloud and Rain Lab
exploration.subject: Earth science
exploration.summary: Predict, then test how parcel cooling forms a visible cloud and how particle growth and evaporation affect rain at the ground.
exploration.question: When does invisible water vapor form a visible cloud, and when does liquid precipitation reach the ground?
exploration.explanation: Water vapor is an invisible gas. As a rising parcel expands and cools, its saturation vapor pressure decreases and relative humidity rises. At saturation, some vapor can condense on particles into visible liquid droplets while condensation and evaporation both continue. A warm cloud still needs particle growth—often collision and coalescence—before liquid precipitation falls; a drier layer below cloud can completely evaporate falling drops into virga. Real clouds may contain liquid droplets, ice crystals or both. This bounded warm-cloud teaching model uses one numerical saturation crossing, fixed cooling rates, a chosen representative particle size and an invented evaporation-path coefficient. It is not a forecast.

experiments.title: Lift to saturation
experiments.instruction: Predict first. Start with 400 m of parcel lift, then change only lift to 1,600 m. Hold starting temperature at 24 °C, starting relative humidity at 60%, particle diameter at 20 µm and below-cloud relative humidity at 80%.
experiments.observe: Compare parcel temperature, relative humidity, estimated cloud base and condensed liquid water. Explain why cooling to saturation can turn some invisible vapor into visible liquid droplets without making precipitation-sized particles.

experiments.title: Grow precipitation
experiments.instruction: Predict first. In the same saturated warm cloud, start with 20 µm droplets, then change only representative particle diameter to 1,000 µm. Hold lift, temperature and both relative-humidity settings fixed.
experiments.observe: Both states keep the same saturated cloud and modeled condensate. Compare the particle's 125,000-fold volume change and estimated diameter at ground level. Explain why cloud droplets must grow, and why evaporation below cloud can produce virga.

exploration.misconception: Air does not literally hold water. Relative humidity compares actual vapor pressure with saturation vapor pressure at the same temperature. A visible cloud consists of liquid droplets, ice crystals or both—not the invisible vapor itself—and not every cloud produces rain at the ground.
